So, the Bible only mentions Eve.
However, there are two ostensibly
contradictory creation accounts at the
beginning of Genesis. One runs from
Genesis 1:1 to the beginning of Genesis
2:4. And then the other runs from the
second half of Genesis 2:4 to the end of
Genesis 3. And in the Genesis 1 creation
account, you have humanity being created
in verses 26 and 27 simultaneously.
But in the Genesis 2 creation account,
you have the man being created first and
then the woman Eve being separated off
from the man secondarily. And so within
early Judaism, there were a bunch of
different ways to approach interpreting
this ostensible contradiction. So for
instance, one way was to understand the
creation of humanity in Genesis 1:26 and
27 as the creation of a single being
made up of two sexes. And then Genesis 2
was the separation of the two sexes into
two separate beings. That was one way to
harmonize the creation accounts. Another
way was to suggest that the creation of
the male and the female humans in
Genesis 1:26 and 27 was the initial
couple, the initial human pair, but then
the woman left for some reason. And then
in Genesis 2, God creates a second woman
from Adam's side. And this is Eve. So
according to that early Jewish
tradition, Adam had a first wife who for
some reason left and then Eve was the
second wife. And then centuries later,
they came up with an explanation for who
that was and why she left.

So this tradition originates in a text
called the alphabet of Ben Sira. And it
was written somewhere between around 700
and 1,000 CE. And this discussion kind
of glosses over the details because the
reality is Lilith wants to be on top.
She does not want to lie below. This is
about sex. And in that time period, as
sometimes even today, sexual position
was a reflection of social hierarchy of
domination versus submission. So to
submit to Adam here is referencing
Lilith's desire to not be on the bottom
during sex. And this was a big deal in
the ancient world. In fact, you had a
bunch of texts that condemned men being
on the bottom during sex with their own
wives during perfectly cromulent sex.
And so it was considered to subordinate,
submit, emasculate, feminize the man. So
you have an ancient Mesopotamian sex
omen that says if a man is on the bottom
during sex, he will lose his personal
deity for a month. And that's a way to
refer to his vitality, his vigor. And
then you have a Jewish text that says if
a man is on the bottom, uh he will be
stricken with delaria, which is an
Aramaic Hebrew word that scholars think
probably refers to diarrhea. So this was
a big deal for them anciently. But in
this text, Lilith is challenging this
socioexual hierarchy. And Adam doesn't
like it. He says, "You are not fit to be
on top. Only I am fit to be on top." So
she storms off and God sends three
angels after her, Senoi, Sansenoi, and
Samangalof. And she refuses to come
back. And that's where we get the next
part of the story.

So when the three angels come to get
Lilith, she says, "I'm not going back. I
am going to be a succubus who uh
afflicts men in the night and who kills
newborn babies. Unless those babies have
an amulet with your three names on it,
Seno, Sansoi, and Samangalof.
if they have that amulet, I will be
powerless against them for the first
eight days of their life. And the idea
would be that on the eighth day, at
least male babies would be circumcised
and then they would be under God's
protection. And so this is probably an
ideology or an origin story for the
practice of using protective amulets
specifically with those three angels
names on them to try to protect babies
from harm in the first few days of their
lives. But this tradition of Lilith as
the first wife of Adam who refuses to
submit to Adam and then runs off and
becomes this demon originates in this
story the alphabet of Ben Sira which was
probably written around 700 to 1,000 CE
and then has taken on a life of its own
